transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-08
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 mins
Recording: https://redwood-recordings/ff/2026-11-08-harborview
Attendees: Liam Ortega (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marco Ruiz (CTO, Harborview), Samantha Lee (Lead ML Eng), Daniel Park (SRE)

[00:00] Liam: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check, audio okay?
[00:05] Marco: Yep, good here.
[00:12] Priya: Awesome. We'll try to keep to 45, 50 if needed. We have the latest bench runs in the shared sheet, link in chat.
[00:20] Samantha: saw it. Noticed the 95th pct latency jump around 2k tokens, yeah.
[00:29] Liam: Right, so main agenda — we dug into the head to head vs CloudAI across the same prompt set, same concurrency. We saw a 12% higher p95 on our config on medium sequences, and throughput capping around 520 TPS earlier than baseline. We want to triage root cause and agree actions.
[01:02] Marco: Quick context — our incumbent is CloudAI, running their hosted endpoints with reserved capacity. Our target is <120ms p95 for typical user flows and sustained 400 TPS with 3 replicas.
[01:22] Daniel: Also want to keep cost per token near current baseline, otherwise ops won't sign off.
[01:28] Priya: Totally. We brought two things to check: batching and KV/prefix cache behavior during the runs, and a quick quantization check to see if int8 paths change tail latency.
[01:44] Samantha: Show us the KV traces — we saw some misses that seemed correlated to the latency spikes.
[01:50] Priya: Yeah so we captured kv-hit metrics, the first run had suboptimal hit-rate because of tokenization differences and prompt canonicalization. There was a small mismatch — CloudAI's tokenizer normalizes punctuation differently, so cache keys weren't aligning 1:1.
[02:20] Marco: Wait, tokenizer mismatch? Is that something we can fix client-side?
[02:27] Priya: In many cases yes, by normalizing or using a shared canonicalization pre-step. We're going to add a normalization shim to the script. That should improve prefix cache hit rate and reduce repeated full compute.
[02:42] Liam: To be clear, that explains part of the p95 delta but not the throughput plateau. Priya, you want to take throughput?
[02:50] Priya: Sure. Throughput capped earlier because our batching policy used a cap of 16 tokens per batch for latency SLOs. The baseline had a slightly higher batch cap and more aggressive async filling. We intentionally tuned for latency, but we can experiment with stepping the batch cap to 20 and enabling adaptive time-window filling. That may push throughput up closer to 650 TPS with a small increase in median latency.
[03:23] Samantha: If we push batch cap, median latency increases — our product team will measure end-to-end user perceived latency. We need to see p95 impact more than median.
[03:33] Priya: Agreed. We'll run a sensitivity matrix: batch cap 16/18/20, adaptive fill on/off, and compare p50/p95/p99 and unit cost.
[03:45] Daniel: Also curious about model variant — which quantization did you use? We saw one run labeled q4_0 and another q5_1?
[03:53] Priya: We used q5_1 in the primary run. We also did an int8-like path for a subset (the compiler path uses optimized kernels) — that showed reduced median lat but some p99 jitter. Quantization may cause kernel scheduling variance on the GPU. We'll include the kernel-level traces.
[04:12] Marco: Kernel scheduling variance — could that be hardware or runtime?
[04:16] Priya: A mix. On our infra the scheduler sometimes fragments when you have mixed small and large sequences; continuous batching helps but also cache warmup matters.
[04:27] Liam: On the question of dedicated capacity — Harborview asked about a small dedicated slot for bursty traffic. We estimated a 2-slot dedicated pool (N=2 gpus) would give a more predictable tail but cost more. Thoughts?
[04:42] Marco: We may be OK with a reserved slot if it solves p95. Need numbers.
[04:47] Liam: We'll send a modeled cost delta for 2 vs 4 slots and an SLA note.
[04:52] Samantha: Back to the bench — there was a note about request shaping, were you doing a constant QPS or a ramp?
[04:58] Priya: We did both. The head-to-head used a fixed concurrency trace matching production: bursts with 10s spikes every 2 minutes. The plateau showed during sustained bursts.
[05:12] Samantha: The plateau happened after about 12 minutes in the run where both systems stabilized. CloudAI held at ~780 TPS for a while, Redwood at 520.
[05:24] Priya: Right. Adding to that, we saw the backend did a few fallback model swaps in the baseline test — baseline had an auto-fallback to a smaller context model during long sequences which kept throughput up. We didn't enable that variant swap in the Redwood run because we wanted consistent model semantics. Should we enable a variant with fallback?
[05:46] Marco: If the smaller-variant fallback changes outputs significantly, it's risky. We want consistent semantics. But if it's for long tails only maybe acceptable with A/B checks.
[05:58] Liam: We can enable controlled fallback and bind it to a canary route so you can eval quality impact.
[06:05] Samantha: Good. Please add an eval harness against our golden prompt set.
[06:10] Priya: Noted. We'll include the eval harness.
[06:14] Daniel: On the security side, Marco asked about audit logs and KMS integration earlier. Any updates?
[06:19] Liam: We have KMS integration for Private installs; for Dedicated we can bring KMS via a customer key pair. We'll attach SOC2 report and the security checklist after the call.
[06:27] Marco: Great, that helps procurement.
[06:30] Priya: I want to walk through the new bench run plan so everyone has clarity — three targeted experiments: 1) Tokenization normalization + KV trace to measure hit rate improvement; 2) Batch cap sweep (16/18/20) with adaptive fill; 3) Controlled fallback variant enabled for long sequences with eval traffic. Each experiment will be a 30-minute run to reach steady state.
[06:59] Samantha: Sounds good. How will we capture traces? Do you need us to enable anything on our end?
[07:06] Priya: We'll need KV tracing enabled and a light agent to capture scheduling/kernels. We'll provide a script that toggles tracing flags; it's not invasive but requires one small env var on the client harness.
[07:19] Daniel: We'll stand that up in our staging cluster. Expect a window Friday-Sunday for runs.
[07:25] Liam: We'll coordinate timing — Priya will drop the script by EOD tomorrow.
[07:29] Priya: I'll put it in the shared folder with run commands and a sample server config.
[07:34] Marco: Quick question on metrics: cost per 1M tokens — can you provide the unit economics for each scenario? Baseline vs dedicated vs fallback-enabled?
[07:44] Liam: Yes, we'll provide an apples-to-apples cost model showing tokens, GPU-hours, and estimated monthly run-rate for your traffic profile.
[07:51] Samantha: When you say unit cost model, make sure to include the impact of KV cache hit improvement — that seems like a key lever.
[07:58] Priya: We'll include that as a sensitivity factor — 10%/20%/30% cache hit improvement and resulting cost delta.
[08:06] Marco: Any red flags or unknowns today?
[08:10] Priya: Unknown: exact tokenization normalization impact and whether the scheduling jitter is reproducible on your staging infra. Both we can test. Minor: quantization path p99 jitter — we'll test alternate quant configs.
[08:22] Liam: Ok let's go through the current run artifacts. Priya, can you summarize the key traces we captured?
[08:27] Priya: Sure. We captured: 1) request latency timeline with per-model latency; 2) KV-hit trace with keys hashed and matching rate; 3) GPU kernel latency histograms; 4) queue length over time. The KV hit-rate in run A was 42% vs baseline's 71% — that's a big lever.
[08:52] Samantha: 42% is a surprise; why so low?
[08:56] Priya: Two reasons: prompt canonicalization differences and a TTL in our cache test was set short to emulate churn. We'll rerun with longer TTL and canonicalization shim.
[09:07] Daniel: TTL was 30s? In prod it's longer. That would explain misses.
[09:11] Priya: Exactly. We'll mirror your prod TTL.
[09:15] Marco: Good. On schedule — when can we expect the next readout?
[09:20] Liam: We'll run experiments this weekend and reconvene Tuesday. How's Tuesday 14:00 UTC?
[09:26] Marco: Works.
[09:28] Samantha: Works for me.
[09:30] Liam: Great. Any procurement blockers we should know about?
[09:33] Marco: Legal wants encryption at rest and SSO via SAML. Also need a preliminary SLA.
[09:38] Liam: We'll include SAML SSO notes and the SLA draft with pricing.
[09:42] Priya: Quick technical note — we recommend not enabling the quantized int path on the first weekend run; lets get KV normalization and batch sweep first. The quant run will be the fourth experiment.
[09:55] Samantha: OK, keep quant as a controlled later test.
[09:58] Daniel: One more ask — can you include a short run that simulates warm start vs cold start? We see user sessions with idle gaps, want to see p95 on cold cache.
[10:07] Priya: We'll add a 10-minute cold-start test where we flush KV and then run bursts.
[10:12] Liam: Recap: Priya drops scripts by 2026-11-09, Redwood runs coordination and cost model, Harborview runs three 30-min tests and uploads traces by 2026-11-13, next meeting Tuesday 2026-11-10 at 14:00 UTC.
[10:27] Marco: Wait, earlier we said Tuesday the 10th — that's fine.
[10:32] Samantha: minor nit — can you also provide a raw CSV of per-request latencies for our analysis?
[10:37] Priya: Yes, we'll include raw CSVs and a short README for fields.
[10:41] Liam: Anything else before we wrap?
[10:44] Marco: No, that's it. Looking forward to the KV improvement numbers.
[10:47] Samantha: thanks all.
[10:50] Liam: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in chat with links and timelines.
[10:53] --- End meeting transcript ---
